Essas licenças são para armas de caça e esporte destinadas a pessoas físicas e distribuidores autorizados. Não acreditamos que exista risco real de desvio para uso militar.'

article_content: A 19-year-old woman from northern China has died in Beijing from H5N1 bird flu, the World Health Organization (WHO) reported Wednesday. The victim, identified as Huang Yanqing, was hospitalized on December 27 and died Monday morning, according to China's state-run Xinhua news agency. Huang reportedly had close contact with ducks at a market in Hebei Province, adjacent to Beijing, on December 19. She purchased nine ducks from the market, cleaned the dead birds, and then distributed them to relatives and friends, Xinhua said. Despite close contact with 116 people, only Huang fell ill, according to the Beijing Municipal Health Bureau. Authorities have disinfected and isolated her home. Zhao Qingchao, a local government official in Langfang City where the market is located, said measures are being taken to trace the virus source. No other cases of H5N1 avian influenza have been reported in the area, Xinhua noted. While officials met in Beijing to discuss the case, the market continues to sell ducks. Globally, H5N1 has caused 248 deaths since 2003, including 21 in China, according to WHO.

CANBERRA, Australia — An eruption at Papua New Guinea’s tallest volcano, Mount Ulawun, intensified regional tsunami concerns before subsiding on Tuesday. Still, thick ash continued to billow skyward, blanketing nearby roofs and palm trees.

Mount Ulawun, one of the South Pacific nation’s most active volcanoes, began erupting on Monday, sending ash clouds as high as 15 kilometers (50,000 feet). Papua New Guinea’s Geohazards Management Division reported that although the eruption level had decreased since Monday’s highest alert, there were no signs of the event ending. 

The remote northeastern island eruption drew international attention, especially when Japanese officials assessed potential tsunami risks for the Izu and Ogasawara islands. However, several volcanologists doubted the volcano would ever pose such a threat. The Geohazards Division noted that the potential for a tsunami was "nil." Brad Scott, a volcanologist with New Zealand’s GNS Science, stated the tsunami risk was "incredibly minor" due to the volcano’s distance from the ocean. 

Despite the reduced alert, Mount Ulawun, which rises 2,334 meters (7,657 feet) above sea level, remained active with the possibility the eruption could continue indefinitely. On Tuesday, the Geohazards Division noted the ash plume reached at least 5,000 meters (16,000 feet) before disappearing into atmospheric clouds. Fine volcanic ash can travel vast distances on wind currents and poses a threat to aviation. A thick plume extended tens of kilometers northwest of Ulawun.

The Civil Aviation Safety Authority of Papua New Guinea did not immediately reply to queries about air travel impacts. Data from FlightAware showed normal operations at the nearest major airports in Port Moresby, the capital, and in Honiara, the Solomon Islands capital.

Australia’s Darwin Volcanic Ash Advisory Center, about 2,300 kilometers (1,400 miles) southwest of Ulawun, was among the first to detect the eruption via satellite. Darwin is one of nine global centers that offer aviation industry advice regarding hazardous volcanic ash movement.

The nearest major town is Bialla, situated among palm oil plantations on Mount Ulawun’s slopes, 47 kilometers (29 miles) southwest of the volcano. Hargy Oil Palm Ltd., based in Bialla, didn’t immediately respond to media requests. The division reported heavy black ash causing palm fronds to droop and covering rooftops in the plantations. Bialla’s population exceeds 13,000, according to World Bank data.

Papua New Guinea sits atop the "Ring of Fire," an arc of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean, notorious for earthquakes and volcanic activity. Mount Ulawun has erupted repeatedly since the 1700s, with its last major activity in 2019 prompting the evacuation of more than 5,000 people. The Geohazards Division reported no known casualties from Ulawun’s eruptions, but significant impacts—including displacement, infrastructure damage, and service disruption—are common.

A Papua Nova Guiné está localizada no "Círculo de Fogo", um arco de falhas sísmicas ao redor do Pacífico conhecido por terremotos e vulcões. article_content: Police chiefs in Germany are planning to abandon a scheme to replace sniffer dogs with vultures after it proved to be unsuccessful. Authorities had imported the birds from Carinthia, Austria, inspired by reports of their excellent eyesight and keen sense of smell. It was hoped that these abilities, along with their natural instinct to discover carcasses, would help police locate dead bodies. However, the three vultures—named Sherlock, Miss Marple, and Columbo—were unable to find any cadavers set out for them during trials. One vulture, Sherlock, rarely flew and instead walked slowly, making him far less efficient than a sniffer dog. The other two birds, Miss Marple and Columbo, spent most of their time fighting each other. An individual involved in the project in Walsrode, Lower Saxony, described the efforts as a ‘disaster’. Early trials with the birds, each with a five-foot wingspan, had already drawn criticism from supporters of traditional methods. One critic noted, ‘Everyone knows what vultures do when they find a body, and they’re much harder to control than a Labrador. Evidence could easily be lost.’ The project’s creator, Hermann Meyer, declined to comment when recently contacted by journalists. Trainer German Alonso admitted the birds ‘don’t seem to be able to do anything other than attack each other’. Research also revealed that vultures may not have been the best candidates, as they tend to be timid and prefer hiding in the woods instead of searching in the open.

Esperava-se que essas habilidades, juntamente com o instinto natural de localizar carcaças, ajudassem a polícia a encontrar corpos. No entanto, os três abutres — chamados Sherlock, Miss Marple e Columbo — não conseguiram localizar nenhum cadáver deixado para eles durante os testes. Um dos abutres, Sherlock, raramente voava e preferia andar devagar, tornando-o muito menos eficiente do que um cão farejador. Os outros dois, Miss Marple e Columbo, passavam a maior parte do tempo brigando entre si. Uma pessoa envolvida no projeto em Walsrode, Baixa Saxônia, descreveu o esforço como um 'desastre'. Os testes iniciais com as aves, cada uma com envergadura de cerca de um metro e meio, já haviam recebido críticas de defensores dos métodos tradicionais. Um dos críticos afirmou: 'Todos sabem o que abutres fazem quando encontram um corpo, e eles são muito mais difíceis de controlar do que um labrador. As evidências poderiam facilmente desaparecer.' O criador do projeto, Hermann Meyer, recusou-se a comentar quando procurado recentemente por jornalistas. O treinador German Alonso admitiu que as aves 'não parecem ser capazes de fazer nada além de brigar entre si'. Pesquisas também mostraram que talvez os abutres não fossem a melhor escolha, pois tendem a ser tímidos e preferem se esconder na floresta a procurar em campo aberto.

article_content: Last night, masked gunmen on a motorbike attacked guests leaving a Coptic wedding at the Virgin Mary Church in Cairo’s Waraa neighborhood, killing three people—including an eight-year-old girl—and injuring a dozen others. The Ministry of Health reported that a man and child died at the scene and a woman succumbed to her injuries en route to the hospital. This was the first deadly assault targeting Christians in Cairo since the military ousted the country’s former Islamist president in July. Prime Minister Hazem el-Beblawi denounced the shooting, calling it a ‘callous and criminal act.’ He promised that the government would pursue those responsible and insisted such attacks would not succeed in dividing Egypt’s Muslims and Christians. Since the military coup, attacks against Egypt’s Coptic Christian minority have risen. Hundreds of people gathered outside the Virgin Mary church in mourning and protest after the shooting. A witness recounted to the BBC that he found a woman covered in blood with multiple gunshot wounds, surrounded by wounded people, including a child. Meanwhile, ongoing clashes between riot police and supporters of ousted President Mohammed Morsi continued at Al-Azhar University, which is closely linked to his Muslim Brotherhood movement. Protesters threw stones, smashed university property, and were besieged by security forces. The unrest is near a site previously cleared by security forces in August, leaving hundreds dead. Student protests began with a march on campus, escalating to property damage, and continued with prayers for dead students at the main gate. These events come amid contentious debate over new protest laws that could bring stricter penalties for demonstrators. Following Morsi’s removal on July 3, Cairo has seen persistent protests and a security crackdown resulting in numerous deaths and arrests. Militant attacks have grown, particularly in Sinai. Recently, Egypt’s interior minister survived a car bombing, and two security officers were wounded when their bus was shot at near Rafah in northern Sinai.

O Ministério da Saúde informou que um homem e uma criança morreram no local, e uma mulher faleceu a caminho do hospital. Este foi o primeiro ataque fatal contra cristãos no Cairo desde que o ex-presidente islâmico foi deposto pelos militares em julho. O primeiro-ministro Hazem el-Beblawi condenou o atentado, classificando-o como um ‘ato cruel e criminoso’. Ele prometeu que o governo vai responsabilizar os autores e garantiu que esses ataques não vão dividir muçulmanos e cristãos no Egito. Após o golpe militar, aumentaram os ataques contra a minoria cristã copta. Centenas se reuniram em luto e protesto na frente da Igreja Virgem Maria após o ataque. Uma testemunha disse à BBC que encontrou uma mulher coberta de sangue e com vários ferimentos de bala, ao lado de outros feridos, inclusive uma criança. Enquanto isso, continuam os confrontos entre policiais de choque e apoiadores do ex-presidente Mohammed Morsi na Universidade Al-Azhar, ligada à Irmandade Muçulmana. Os manifestantes atiraram pedras, danificaram propriedades da universidade e foram cercados pelas forças de segurança. Esse local fica ao lado de uma área que foi alvo de intervenção policial em agosto, deixando centenas de mortos. Os protestos estudantis começaram com uma marcha no campus, passaram para depredação e seguiram diante do portão principal com orações pelos estudantes mortos. Esses episódios ocorrem em meio à discussão de leis mais duras para manifestações, que prevêem punições severas para protestos não autorizados. Após a saída de Morsi em 3 de julho, o Cairo passou a registrar manifestações frequentes e forte repressão policial, resultando em diversas mortes e prisões. Ataques de militantes avançaram, especialmente no Sinai. Recentemente, o ministro do Interior sobreviveu a um carro-bomba e dois agentes de segurança ficaram feridos quando o ônibus em que estavam foi atacado perto de Rafah, no norte do Sinai.

NASA's Curiosity rover is set for a spectacular landing on Mars at 1:31 a.m. ET Monday, marking a pivotal event in planetary exploration. Costing $2.6 billion and roughly the size of an SUV, Curiosity will arrive amid the highly anticipated 'seven minutes of terror,' a daring landing sequence involving a sky crane and the world's largest supersonic parachute. These mechanisms will guide the spacecraft to Gale Crater, a site carefully selected for its scientific importance.

According to NASA, Curiosity is healthy and on course, having departed Earth on November 26. The rover is operated from NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory and boasts an impressive suite of scientific equipment: 17 cameras, a laser for remote rock analysis, and instruments to study soil and rock samples. 

Curiosity's first destination is Gale Crater, thought to have once held a lake. After at least a year, the rover will travel to Mount Sharp, in the crater's center, to study its layered sediments. Each layer could reveal an era in Mars' history, similar to Earth’s sedimentary records found in locations like Death Valley or Glacier National Park, though Mars lacks plate tectonics, resulting in undisturbed, flat layers. This suggests Mount Sharp formed differently than mountains on Earth, though the exact process remains unclear, says chief scientist John Grotzinger.

Scientists are particularly interested in detecting organic molecules within these layers. While organics are essential for life, their presence alone is not proof of life, emphasizes Steve Squyres from the mission's science team, as such molecules can also be formed abiotically. If organics are absent, it could indicate unknown factors destroying them, notes James Wray of Georgia Tech. 

A successful landing would reassure the Mars science community and maintain NASA’s position as a leader in Mars exploration, Wray adds. Scientists do not expect to find surface liquid water on Mars, given the planet's cold, arid conditions; if it exists, it would be deep underground and out of Curiosity’s reach.

Rock dating on Mars is challenging, so it is difficult to determine when water may have existed there. Data suggests that Mars’ 'warm and wet' period lasted through the planet's first billion years. Life requires both a suitable environment, such as the presence of water, and organic building blocks, says Squyres. The mission aims to explore a promising location with advanced tools, rather than target specific molecules.

The Jet Propulsion Laboratory buzzed with activity as media, scientists, and celebrities gathered ahead of the landing, reflecting widespread public interest. Watch parties worldwide, such as at the Georgia Institute of Technology’s Atlanta Science Tavern, brought together science enthusiasts eager to witness history in the making.

As part of tradition, NASA staff passed around peanuts for good luck, a custom said to improve mission outcomes, according to lead flight director David Oh. The landing also coincides with former astronaut Neil Armstrong’s 82nd birthday, an auspicious date, according to NASA’s John Grunsfeld.

Curiosity is designed to operate for two years, but might surpass that target. Past rovers Spirit and Opportunity outlasted their expected lifespans; Opportunity continues operating even today, while Spirit fell silent in 2010 after becoming stuck. 'You take what Mars gives you,' says Squyres, lead scientist for previous rover missions. 'If we knew what we were going to find, it wouldn’t be this much fun.'

article_content: In Atlanta, Kirsten Ott and Maria Palladino celebrated their commitment with a wedding that mixed timeless traditions and their unique style. Kirsten wore a classic white gown and Maria donned a white suit, and together they exchanged vows before family and friends—even though Georgia didn’t recognize same-sex marriage at the time. Finding welcoming vendors was a challenge. Worried about possible rejection, the couple reached out to potential providers mostly by email. Some vendors did not reply, but persistence led them to open-minded businesses, including a photographer who had worked with LGBTQ+ couples and a venue—the Mary Gay House—that welcomed them. When searching for ideas in wedding magazines, Kirsten and Maria were disappointed to see no representation of gay couples. Feeling largely invisible in mainstream wedding culture, they decided to fill this void. Combining Kirsten’s background in journalism and Maria’s graphic design skills, they founded Equally Wed, an online magazine dedicated to supporting same-sex weddings. Equally Wed helps LGBTQ+ couples find friendly vendors across the country, from cake bakers to florists and jewelers such as Rony Tennenbaum, who designs custom rings while challenging stereotypes about same-sex weddings. The magazine’s staff researches inclusive businesses and connects couples to venues and honeymoon destinations. Spotlighting businesses like Atlanta’s Le Tux Shop, which tailors suits for women and offers alternative attire for bridal parties, the magazine showcases options beyond traditional norms. Kirsten explains their mission was to give same-sex couples planning weddings visibility and assurance that their celebrations are valid. Maria notes most gay weddings resemble straight weddings apart from small details, like who walks down the aisle. At that point, same-sex marriage had been legalized in Massachusetts, Connecticut, Vermont, Iowa, New Hampshire, and Washington D.C., with New Jersey recognizing civil unions. Despite the legal uncertainties, Kirsten stresses that what truly matters is pledging your life to someone you love in front of supportive friends and family.

article_content: NASA has reported suspected sabotage after discovering cut wires in a noncritical piece of hardware designated for launch to the International Space Station (ISS) on space shuttle Endeavour. The tampered equipment was part of a system meant to relay sensor data from the ISS to ground control. NASA has launched a formal investigation into the matter. Endeavour’s upcoming mission is set for August 7, marking its first journey after almost five years and a comprehensive rebuilding process following the Columbia disaster in 2003. This will be NASA’s second shuttle flight of the year. On this trip, Endeavour will deliver an important support beam and a replacement gyroscope to the $100-billion ISS, helping the orbital laboratory keep its proper orientation. The spacecraft is also transporting about 5,000 pounds of equipment and supplies for the current station crew. The shuttle features a new power transfer system enabling it to draw electricity from the ISS. If the system performs well, the mission could be extended from 11 to 14 days, allowing the crew to finish preparations for upcoming laboratories from Europe and Japan. The crew of seven includes teacher-astronaut Barbara Morgan, who was once backup for Christa McAuliffe—the educator lost in the Challenger tragedy of 1986. Shuttle program manager Wayne Hale compared the revamped Endeavour to a 'brand new car,' highlighting its complete overhaul. The sabotage inquiry is ongoing, with NASA focused on ensuring crew safety and mission success.

Vivianne Miedema, Arsenal's prolific striker, has been called up to the Netherlands national team for their upcoming UEFA Women's Nations League matches, despite not yet playing for her club since suffering an ACL injury last December. Miedema sustained the injury during a Champions League match against Olympique Lyonnais on December 15, 2022, which was the first major setback in her career and was projected to keep her sidelined for nine months.

Dutch national team coach Andries Jonker included Miedema in the squad after consulting with both Arsenal and Miedema herself. He stated that Miedema has been training with Arsenal and, if things continue to progress well, she may feature in the matches against Scotland. Arsenal manager Jonas Eidevall confirmed collaborative discussions took place with the Dutch coaching staff and said that Miedema is very close to being ready for competitive play, possibly even returning to Arsenal’s squad soon.

Miedema previously ruled herself out of the FIFA Women's World Cup in July, stating that she needed to be realistic about her recovery timeline and hoped to return at the start of the next club season. So far, five games into the new season, she has not yet appeared for Arsenal, though her teammate and partner, Beth Mead, recently returned from a similar injury.

Eidevall explained that although Miedema initially hoped to regain match fitness with Arsenal’s second team, this has proven difficult due to the pitches used for their home games. Instead, the club has organized internal practice matches to better simulate a competitive environment and aid Miedema's gradual return. Miedema has emphasized she will not rush her recovery and aims to be fully fit before returning to action, with the December international break identified as a possible target for her comeback with the national team.

The UK Government has supported a recent EU decision that could allow genetically modified (GM) maize, designed to resist weedkillers, to be planted in England as early as next year. EU agriculture ministers approved a policy letting individual member states choose whether or not to grow GM crops. Scotland and Wales, for example, have chosen to maintain bans.

Environmental organizations and opponents of GM crops have strongly criticized the move, arguing it could harm wildlife, cause cross-contamination with conventional and organic crops, and create economic challenges for farmers. Surveys suggest that many people in England are also concerned about the potential environmental and health effects of GM agriculture.

Environment Secretary Owen Paterson has actively campaigned for EU rules that give countries the power to approve GM crops after they’ve passed the EU’s safety checks. Paterson contends that the EU’s new approach will streamline the approval process, advance scientific innovation, and provide farmers with more choices.

Multinational biotech companies have lobbied UK officials to speed up GM crop approvals, working closely with the government since a 2012 summit organized by the Agricultural Biotechnology Council. Some scientific reviews supportive of GM crops have been authored by individuals with industry connections.

While government officials argue that GM crops are safe for people and the environment, critics cite European and US studies that raise concerns about health risks, impact on biodiversity, and the emergence of herbicide-resistant weeds. The government has promised safeguards against GM contamination of non-GM crops, but campaigners remain unconvinced.

article_content: Cristian Grigore Spiridon, a 35-year-old Romanian singer and semi-finalist on Britain's Got Talent, reportedly owes £25,000 to Eurovision singer Mihai Trăistariu over false claims of a romantic affair. The controversy began three years ago when Spiridon was taken to a Romanian civil court after alleging in the local newspaper Cancan that he had a relationship with Trăistariu. Trăistariu, who represented Romania at Eurovision in 2006, denied the claims, stating they had only met once at a group event and never spoke. He won the court case, but says the compensation was never paid, as Spiridon 'vanished' after the ruling. A friend of Spiridon stated that he admits to making the claim and regrets his actions, but believes the newspaper should be responsible for the payment. Despite ongoing controversy and criticism from Britain's Got Talent judges Amanda Holden, Alesha Dixon, and Simon Cowell, comedian David Walliams was impressed by Spiridon's performance of 'Sex Bomb' by Sir Tom Jones, awarding him the Golden Buzzer to move on to the next round. Spiridon previously auditioned for The X Factor, appearing in red underpants and performing Kylie Minogue's 'I Can't Get You Out Of My Head,' but did not progress. MailOnline has contacted Britain's Got Talent for comment.

article_content: Britain is aiming to be the first country outside the United States to open a spaceport, with space tourism flights from the UK expected as early as 2018. The UK government unveiled this initiative at the Farnborough Air Show in Hampshire, revealing eight possible sites—one each in England and Wales, and six in Scotland—even with the Scottish independence referendum on the horizon. Business Secretary Vince Cable highlighted that the UK space sector contributes $19 billion (£11.3 billion) a year and supports nearly 35,000 jobs. While Britain has previously taken part in space launches from Australia, it now has a more ambitious objective: to secure 10% of the global space market, raising the sector’s value to $68 billion annually. Science Minister David Willetts stated that the government has developed the necessary regulatory and aviation procedures for launches and has identified a shortlist of sites. He emphasized his goal for the UK space sector to outpace China’s economy in growth. This announcement reflects strong optimism and progress within the UK’s space industry. The British firm Reaction Engines recently introduced a pioneering, pilotless reusable spacecraft designed for conventional take-off and landing. Alan Bond, director and inventor at Reaction Engines, noted that the spaceport is the culmination of years of investment, and suggested that Britain could be a world leader in space science per capita, previously held back only by launch technology. Continued government funding is helping the sector move forward. International leaders in space tourism, including Virgin Galactic led by Richard Branson and XCOR, are anticipated to use the new spaceport. With Branson expressing interest in a UK location, increased competition and infrastructure are expected to lower the current $204,000 cost for a Virgin Galactic flight, potentially by as much as 80%, according to the Space Innovation and Growth Strategy board. This could trigger heightened competition for a stake in the growing space sector. As commercial space travel becomes more accessible, more people may soon be able to realize their dream of visiting space.

O secretário de Negócios, Vince Cable, destacou que o setor espacial britânico movimenta US$ 19 bilhões (£11,3 bilhões) por ano e emprega cerca de 35 mil pessoas. Apesar de participar anteriormente de lançamentos espaciais na Austrália, o Reino Unido agora tem um objetivo mais ousado: conquistar 10% do mercado espacial global e elevar o valor do setor para US$ 68 bilhões anuais. O ministro da Ciência, David Willetts, afirmou que o governo já elaborou os procedimentos regulatórios e de aviação necessários para os lançamentos e identificou uma lista restrita de locais. Ele destacou que seu objetivo é fazer com que o setor espacial britânico cresça mais rápido do que a economia chinesa. O anúncio reflete o otimismo e o avanço do setor espacial do Reino Unido. article_content: Humza Yousaf's in-laws have returned to Scotland after being trapped in Gaza for four weeks. The family of Scotland's First Minister reunited after the couple managed to cross into Egypt on Friday. Elizabeth El-Nakla and her husband, Maged – the parents of Mr Yousaf's wife Nadia – were allowed to leave Gaza through the Rafah crossing. Mr Yousaf confirmed the news on X, formerly known as Twitter, and posted a photo of their reunion. He stated: 'I am pleased to say my in-laws are safe and back home.' The post included Arabic text translating to 'praise be to God.' Some of Mr Yousaf's relatives, who do not hold UK passports, remain in Gaza. Mr Yousaf added: 'We are, of course, elated, but my father-in-law said, "My heart is broken in two, and with my mum, son, and grandchildren in Gaza." He became emotional, describing how hard it was to say goodbye.' He continued: 'Our thoughts remain with those who can't leave and are trapped in a war zone. We will continue to call for peace and an end to the killing of innocent men, women, and children in Gaza. This has been a traumatic few weeks, with a significant impact on Nadia and our family, particularly my in-laws. I'm sure they will share their story with time. Meanwhile, we ask for privacy.' The couple traveled to Gaza early last month to visit Mr El-Nakla's mother, who had a stroke in March but has since recovered. Mr Yousaf's brother-in-law, a hospital doctor, and his family remain in Gaza, as do his wife's stepmother and grandmother. Mr and Mrs El-Nakla, from Dundee, spent the past two weeks sheltering in a house with around 100 people, including a two-month-old baby. They had tried to leave the territory on three previous occasions without success. According to the BBC, the couple arrived at Edinburgh Airport around 10:30 a.m. on Sunday. Border crossings in and out of Gaza had been closed since 7 October, when Hamas, a proscribed terrorist organization in the UK, attacked Israel, killing more than 1,400 people and taking over 240 hostages. Since then, Israel has conducted military operations in Gaza. The Hamas-run health ministry says over 9,700 people have died. The Palestinian border authority has issued lists naming those allowed to cross with their passports. On Friday, the list included more than 90 British citizens, and 88 on Saturday's list. Deputy Prime Minister Oliver Dowden confirmed on Sunday that over 100 UK citizens have left Gaza. Before the conflict, there were estimated to be around 200 British nationals in the territory. Up to 500 foreign nationals have been leaving Gaza daily through the Rafah crossing into Egypt since Wednesday, but evacuations were paused on Saturday. A source told the BBC these were expected to resume on Sunday. Evacuations have been conducted during specific, limited time periods, under the control of Egyptian authorities. On Saturday, hundreds of pro-Palestinian demonstrators marched and staged sit-ins at Edinburgh Waverley and Glasgow railway stations, calling for a ceasefire and for Palestine to be free. In Glasgow, they moved on to the BBC Scotland headquarters for a rally. On Sunday, a silent vigil was held outside the Scottish Parliament in Edinburgh to remember those held hostage by Hamas. Heart-shaped balloons were tied to shoes to symbolize those kidnapped.

Cerca de 500 estrangeiros estavam saindo diariamente de Gaza pela passagem de Rafah, rumo ao Egito, desde quarta-feira, mas as evacuações foram pausadas no sábado. Uma fonte disse à BBC que elas voltariam a ocorrer no domingo. As evacuações estão acontecendo em períodos limitados, sob controle das autoridades egípcias. No sábado, centenas de manifestantes pró-Palestina fizeram protestos e sentadas nas estações ferroviárias de Edimburgo Waverley e Glasgow, pedindo cessar-fogo e liberdade para a Palestina. Em Glasgow, seguiram para a sede da BBC Escócia para um ato. No domingo, uma vigília silenciosa foi realizada em frente ao Parlamento Escocês, em Edimburgo, em homenagem aos reféns do Hamas. Balões em formato de coração foram amarrados a sapatos para simbolizar os sequestrados.

article_content: Hundreds of Sudanese refugees are stranded in the olive groves of Zarzis, Tunisia, fearing local hostility and hoping for protection from the United Nations. Zarzis, a small town known for tourism and fishing near the Libyan border, has become an unexpected destination for these refugees, who fled violence in Sudan and endured perilous journeys through Libya. Farah Mahmoud, 23, left his final year at university in Khartoum after war broke out and arrived in Zarzis after losing his brother in a Libyan detention center. Local shopkeeper Lofti Gheriani has organized community meetings and demonstrations, expressing concern over the refugees' presence and its impact on tourism. Gheriani and other community members have petitioned for the relocation of the UNHCR office, citing pressure on local resources and businesses. The UNHCR in Zarzis is struggling to meet the needs of a growing number of refugees, migrants, and asylum seekers, with significant delays for registration and services. As of October 24 this year, 2,523 people have registered with the UNHCR in Zarzis, with 20% being unaccompanied minors. Many refugees live in makeshift camps in olive groves, facing poor living conditions and uncertainty about their future as they await official UNHCR registration cards. Some, like Elsafi Mohammed Alam, simply seek safety and legal status; others, such as Abdelrahim, recount dangerous journeys and ongoing poverty. Tensions have worsened following political statements from President Kais Saied earlier this year, leading to increased hostility toward Black asylum seekers. The refugee presence has added to local concerns about the already struggling tourism industry, with several hotels closed and business owners reporting declines. Despite promises of increased support, the UNHCR's resources remain stretched, and both refugees and locals face ongoing challenges.

Gheriani e outros membros da comunidade fizeram um abaixo-assinado pedindo a transferência do escritório do ACNUR, alegando pressão sobre os recursos e comércios locais. O ACNUR em Zarzis enfrenta dificuldades para atender ao crescente número de refugiados, migrantes e solicitantes de asilo, com grandes atrasos no registro e nos serviços. Até 24 de outubro deste ano, 2.523 pessoas se registraram no ACNUR em Zarzis, sendo 20% menores desacompanhados. article_content: On Tuesday, Indian equities saw gains despite mixed global signals. Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) were net buyers, investing Rs 783 crore, while domestic institutional investors (DIIs) bought shares worth Rs 1,324 crore. Market participants are closely watching upcoming state exit polls for more direction. Mining stocks are expected to be in focus, with the government set to auction 20 critical and strategic mineral blocks. Auto stocks may also attract attention due to robust sales in November, driven by festive demand, according to Siddhartha Khemka, Head of Retail Research at Motilal Oswal. GIFT Nifty, formerly SGX Nifty, indicated a positive opening for Indian markets, rising 23 points to 20,150.50. Technical analysis suggests a sustained move above 19,900 could lead to new all-time highs, while dips may find support around 19,800-19,750, according to Nagaraj Shetti of HDFC Securities. India VIX, a measure of market volatility, increased by 7.16% to 12.18. In the US, major stocks closed with modest gains—Dow Jones up 0.24%, S&P 500 up 0.10%, and Nasdaq up 0.29%—amid mixed signals from the Federal Reserve and positive consumer data. Asian markets posted mixed results. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.5% after lower inflation data, while Japan’s Topix fell 0.4% and Hang Seng futures declined by 1%. S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 futures both rose by 0.1%. European Euro Stoxx 50 futures were little changed. Oil prices rose after storms in the Black Sea disrupted exports from Kazakhstan and Russia, raising concerns about supply and ahead of a key OPEC+ decision on potential output cuts. Stocks under F&O ban today include Balrampur Chini Mills, BHEL, Indiabulls Housing Finance, and Granules; this status applies when securities exceed 95% of their market-wide position limit. The Indian rupee closed slightly higher at 83.35 per US dollar due to dollar sales by foreign banks and a broadly weaker US dollar. Foreign institutional investors reduced their net short positions in the F&O segment from Rs 1.30 lakh crore on Friday to Rs 1.28 lakh crore on Tuesday. In corporate news, top shareholders at Byju’s have asked the company to meet specific conditions before considering further capital infusion, as the edtech firm faces financial challenges. The increasing popularity of virtual influencers is noted, with brands like Titan, Realme, MG Motors, and Boat using 3D-animated influencers such as Kyra and Naina for online campaigns. Ahmed Hamid Ahmed, an independent director at Religare Enterprises, has questioned the timing of the open offer from the Burman family, calling it 'fishy' in the first such public comment by a board member.

article_content: Sheikh Saud Bin Mohammed Al-Thani, recognized for his significant art collection, is currently involved in a lawsuit over alleged unpaid debts to several major auction houses. He is accused of not paying $19.7 million for a collection of ancient Greek coins from the Prospero Collection, auctioned in New York. Dealers still have possession of the coins but argue that Sheikh Saud is obliged to complete the purchase in line with his winning bid. The dealers’ legal representative, Jeffrey Gruder QC, argues that Sheikh Saud has a history of delayed payments, comparing his behavior to that of a compulsive spender. The dealers involved—A.H. Baldwin and Sons Ltd, Dmitry Markov Coins and Medals, and N&M Numismatics LLC—claim he has not provided a reason for the lack of payment and cite a broader pattern of unsettled debts. The matter is being heard at the UK High Court, where an extension of an existing asset-freezing order is being sought. Sheikh Saud, a member of Qatar’s royal family, allegedly owes significant amounts to Bonhams (£4.3 million), Sotheby's (about $42 million), and other dealers. Gruder argues that the sheikh’s royal status should not impact the legal process. Efforts to resolve the outstanding payment included diplomatic engagement by both UK and Qatari ambassadors, but no payment has been secured to date. Sheikh Saud is well-known for notable acquisitions, such as the £3 million Clive of India Flask, rare photographs, Fabergé eggs, and other valuable pieces. In 2005, Sheikh Saud’s collecting activity was interrupted by house arrest in Qatar over allegations related to invoice reporting. He returned to auction activities shortly thereafter. There are concerns over his current presence outside the UK, but his lawyer Stephen Rubin QC asserts that he is in Doha for personal reasons and not to avoid legal proceedings. Rubin insists that Sheikh Saud has been trying to resolve the payment for the coins, suggesting the situation is due to timing rather than refusal. He further maintains that the dealers have no enforceable contract with the sheikh and are free to sell the coins to another buyer. The judgment from the High Court is pending in this ongoing case concerning these substantial debts.

A CNN feature about Noor al-Zahra Haider, an Iraqi girl who received life-saving medical treatment in the United States during the Iraq War, has prompted widespread concern and offers of help from the public. Many readers felt personally connected to Noor’s challenges and sought ways to support her ongoing care. To facilitate this, Childspring International, an Atlanta-based Christian charity that coordinated Noor’s U.S. medical care in 2006, established the Baby Noor Fund. The fund aims to gather donations specifically for Noor and her family, though how the funds will be used is still being decided—options include connecting them with specialists in Baghdad or sending medical supplies.

Noor was born with acute spina bifida, a serious birth defect affecting her spine. Discovered by U.S. soldiers as a baby in late 2005 during a search operation near Christmas, Noor was deemed unlikely to survive by local doctors. After being brought to the U.S., she underwent surgery that saved her life and returned home after six months. Some observers have questioned whether she should have remained in the United States to receive ongoing care, given the difficulties her family faces in managing her medical needs back in Iraq.

Noor continues to deal with complex health problems. She depends on a brain shunt to control fluid buildup, frequently suffers from infections that endanger her kidneys, and has lost feeling in her lower body, making it impossible to walk. As a result of their connection to American aid, Noor's family has faced threats and had to relocate for safety.

On the 10th anniversary of the Iraq War, Noor’s story reignited discussion among CNN’s readers. Many people offered messages of support, while others debated whether there is a continued moral responsibility to help those like Noor whose lives were changed by war. Some advocate for ongoing support, while others believe resources may be needed more urgently elsewhere. The situation highlights challenging questions about the responsibilities that come with humanitarian intervention and how best to support individuals like Noor in the long-term.

article_content: A team of scientists has developed a novel oil spill dispersant using edible ingredients typically found in foods such as peanut butter, chocolate, and whipped cream. This new solution was created as a safer alternative to traditional dispersants following concerns raised after the Deepwater Horizon spill in 2010. The formula not only breaks apart oil slicks but also stops oil from coating the feathers of birds or harming wildlife. Lisa Kemp from the University of Southern Mississippi presented the research at the American Chemical Society. She noted that all components of the dispersant are safe and common in processed foods. Unlike existing products, this blend both disperses oil and prevents it from sticking to animals or objects—similar to how laundry detergents keep grease off clothes during rinsing. 'Birds can move through the dispersed oil and the substance won’t stick to them,' said Dr. Robert Lochhead, the concept's originator. The formulation includes a polymer that coats oil droplets, preventing them from adhering to feathers or fur, much as detergent polymers do for clothing. This advance could protect wildlife and allow for easier beach cleanup after oil spills. Standard cleaning methods, like detergents, can strip animals' natural waterproofing, making them susceptible to cold and other dangers. Wildlife also risks ingesting oil, which proved lethal for an estimated 225,000 birds during the 1989 Exxon Valdez disaster. An advantage of the new dispersant is that its ingredients are inexpensive and readily available in bulk, making rapid emergency deployment feasible. Kemp suggested that emergency responders, like the U.S. Coast Guard, could keep small stocks for immediate use and quickly scale up as needed. Supported by the National Science Foundation, the researchers used robotic screening to pinpoint the best ingredient combinations and have advanced their blend to a prototype stage ready for large-scale testing. Companies such as Dow, Archer Daniels Midland, and Croda International contributed expertise and resources for ingredient sourcing. The team is now looking to partner with organizations interested in testing and helping bring this environmentally friendly dispersant to broader use.

article_content: An investigation is underway after nearly 160 cases of Salmonella poisoning were reported across the UK, possibly linked to a national outbreak. Public Health England (PHE) is examining cases of Salmonella Enteritidis in Hampshire, London, the West Midlands, Cheshire, and Merseyside. The incidents occurred in isolated clusters over several months, but officials now believe they may be connected. Genetic testing suggests the 156 cases could originate from a single source, according to PHE. PHE is working with the Food Standards Agency and local authorities to determine the cause of the outbreak, which may also involve cases in France and Austria. Dr. Paul Cleary, consultant epidemiologist at PHE, said that the agency is collaborating with national and European public health organizations. He stated progress is being made and that further action will be taken if needed. In Hampshire, 55 cases have been identified, 32 of which are associated with an oriental restaurant. In Cheshire and Merseyside, 33 cases have been reported, with 31 linked to an oriental takeaway. In the West Midlands, 43 cases have been identified, 34 connected to an outbreak at Birmingham Heartlands Hospital. Salmonella symptoms include diarrhea, vomiting, fever, nausea, and stomach cramps. While anyone can contract salmonella, young children, elderly people, and those with weakened immune systems are at greater risk of severe illness. Symptoms usually last four to seven days and often resolve without treatment, though severe cases may require medical care for dehydration. Salmonella can be transmitted through contaminated food (often of animal origin) or via contact with infected people or animals. Heart of England NHS Foundation Trust confirmed the Birmingham hospital outbreak in June; four staff members and 19 patients tested positive for the bacteria. PHE is also investigating 25 reported salmonella cases in London. Salmonella Enteritidis is commonly associated with gastrointestinal illness and often linked to poultry or eggs. Professor Anthony Hilton of Aston University noted that, if the cases are related, identifying common risk factors is the next step. He explained that tracing these factors involves compiling detailed food and exposure histories, which is complex and time-consuming. Authorities continue to monitor the situation to determine the true extent of the outbreak and its source.

article_content: An inquest heard that a 999 emergency call handler, Aaliyah Ormerod, made critical errors during a call concerning a choking baby at a nursery in Cheadle Hulme, Stockport. The incident involved nine-month-old Millie Thompson, who passed away after choking on shepherd’s pie at Ramillies Hall private nursery in October last year. A nursery staff member contacted emergency services and informed Ms Ormerod that Millie was choking, crying, and had become 'a bit purple.' Ms Ormerod collected the necessary information, gave instructions, and reassured that an ambulance was on its way. After ending the call, she was recorded saying, 'Jeez, stop giving me information,' unaware the line was still active. The inquest at Oldham Magistrates’ Court revealed that nursery staff and paramedics, including Paul Williams, could not save Millie. In a statement, Ms Ormerod admitted she did not grasp the seriousness of the situation and made two fundamental errors: not remaining on the line to monitor Millie’s condition and not recognizing the significance of her color change. Following scripted questions, Ms Ormerod advised staff to stop slapping Millie on the back, recommended that Millie not eat or drink, and suggested she be positioned comfortably on her side in case of vomiting. She instructed the nursery to call back immediately if anything changed. A review found that being told the baby was turning purple should have led to a more urgent response, rather than continued scripted questioning. Ms Ormerod later admitted her mistakes and suggested improvements were needed in the call-handling system. Ms Ormerod, not present at the inquest, remains employed with the North West Ambulance Service in a different role. She said the possibility that her actions may have contributed to a death has devastated her. Millie’s parents, Joanne and Dan Thompson, sought answers as to how their healthy daughter failed to return home from nursery. Staff performed first aid while awaiting the ambulance, but Millie suffered cardiac arrest and was pronounced dead at Stepping Hill Hospital about an hour after the incident. Coroner John Pollard noted surprise that no disciplinary action was taken following Ms Ormerod’s inappropriate comment. Angela Lee, section manager in the emergency control room, testified the call should have been classified as a 'red response,' indicating an immediate threat to life requiring arrival within eight minutes. Since the incident, all emergency medical dispatchers have received further training on handling choking cases. Ms Ormerod returned to work six months after the event. Paramedics said Millie was unresponsive when they arrived and could not be revived. The inquest is ongoing.

Ormerod orientou os funcionários a pararem de bater nas costas de Millie, recomendou que ela não comesse ou bebesse nada e que fosse posicionada confortavelmente de lado caso vomitasse. Ela também pediu que ligassem de volta imediatamente se algo mudasse. Uma análise concluiu que, ao ser informada que o bebê estava ficando roxo, uma resposta mais urgente deveria ter sido gerada, ao invés de continuar com perguntas padronizadas. Posteriormente, a Sra. Ormerod reconheceu seus erros e sugeriu melhorias no sistema de atendimento. A Sra. Ormerod, que não esteve presente na investigação, permanece empregada pelo Serviço de Ambulâncias do Noroeste, agora em outro cargo. Ela afirmou que a possibilidade de suas ações terem contribuído para uma morte a deixou devastada. Os pais de Millie, Joanne e Dan Thompson, buscaram respostas sobre como sua filha saudável não retornou da creche. Os funcionários prestaram os primeiros socorros enquanto aguardavam a ambulância, mas Millie sofreu parada cardíaca e foi declarada morta no Hospital Stepping Hill cerca de uma hora após o incidente. O legista John Pollard demonstrou surpresa pelo fato de não ter havido nenhuma medida disciplinar após o comentário inadequado de Sra. Ormerod. Angela Lee, chefe de seção da central de controle de emergências, afirmou que a ligação deveria ter sido tratada como 'resposta vermelha', sinalizando ameaça imediata à vida e exigindo chegada em até oito minutos. Desde o incidente, todos os despachantes de emergência receberam treinamento adicional para casos de engasgo. A Sra. Ormerod voltou ao trabalho seis meses após o ocorrido. Os paramédicos disseram que Millie estava inconsciente ao chegarem e não pôde ser reanimada. A investigação continua.

article_content: A former police officer, Sugra Hanif, 27, from Banbury, Oxfordshire, has been sentenced to three years in prison for accessing the personal details of road crash victims from a Thames Valley Police computer and selling them to compensation lawyers. Hanif carried out the scheme with her married partner, Raza Khan, 27, from Handsworth, Birmingham. Both were sentenced to three years in prison at Winchester Crown Court, where they were told their scam could have netted up to £1 million in referral fees if it had not been uncovered. Hanif previously worked for Thames Valley Police and used her access to the Police National Computer to retrieve details on people involved in car accidents, reportedly accessing 2,456 files. She and Khan then contacted the victims, pressuring them to file accident claims with no-win, no-fee legal firms. Khan's accident claims management business, SR Auto Repairs, received referral fees between £700 and £800 for each claim, earning around £26,400 in seven months. The prosecution estimated their potential earnings could have exceeded £1 million. At sentencing, Judge Andrew Barnett commented that Hanif's actions seriously undermined public trust and were a gross breach of responsibility. He noted, 'You are a disgrace to the uniform you once wore, and you have let down your colleagues and the police service.' Thames Valley Police faces a potential fine of about £500,000 from the Information Commissioner due to the unprecedented data breach. Up to 5,000 people could also pursue legal action against the force. Hanif was dismissed from Thames Valley Police after her conviction, which followed a seven-week trial. She asserted that Khan pressured her into obtaining the data by threatening to reveal their affair to her religious father, and claimed to have been ‘infatuated’ with Khan at the time. Khan denied exerting such pressure. The court heard Khan had previously been sentenced to 42 months in prison in 2008 for causing death by dangerous driving and had other violent offence convictions dating back to 2002. Khan’s wife, Paramjeet Kaur, 26, was tried for conspiracy to commit misconduct in public office but was acquitted after the jury could not reach a verdict.

article_content: Brown sauce, a staple condiment in the UK for over a century, is seeing a notable decline in popularity. According to industry analysts, sales fell by 19% last year, with changing food habits and increased awareness of healthy eating believed to be major factors. Spending on brown sauce decreased by £8 million in the same period. HP Sauce, created in 1895 by Nottingham grocer Frederick Gibson Garton, has long been associated with British culture and referenced in literature and politics. However, data from Mintel shows brown sauce sales dropped from 16 million kilos in 2013 to 13 million kilos last year, with the combined sales value of various brands falling by 17% from £47 million to £39 million. Experts suggest that concerns over salt content, reduced popularity of traditional breakfast fry-ups, and the rise of healthier breakfast options like porridge have driven the decline. Despite the downturn, devoted fans remain loyal. Tom Parker Bowles, a food critic for the Mail on Sunday, commented that classic dishes like fry-ups and bacon sandwiches 'would not be the same' without HP Sauce and called for efforts to 'Save Our Sauce.' Both HP Sauce and tomato ketchup have seen sales decline, although ketchup remains more popular, particularly in fast-food venues. Richard Ford, a senior food analyst at Mintel, noted that the decrease reflects evolving meal preferences with fewer meals requiring table sauces. A Heinz spokesperson, representing the American company that acquired HP in 2005 and also owns Daddies, disputed the figures, suggesting the decline may be due to the popularity of smaller pack sizes, and noted that sales of certain HP sauce bottles have increased by 2%. Currently, most brown sauce, including HP and Daddies, is produced in the Netherlands. Colman's OK sauce is the last major brown sauce made in the UK.

article_content: The F-35C Lightning II, America's costliest weapons program, completed its first-ever landing on an aircraft carrier—the USS Nimitz near San Diego. Despite costing around $400 billion and grappling with delays, technical setbacks, and overspending, this achievement stands as a critical step in the jet’s journey to full deployment. The Pentagon describes this initial carrier landing as a significant leap forward for the F-35C. The jet used a repeatedly redesigned tailhook system—a crucial device tasked with catching wires on the deck to halt the plane—due to development challenges. There are three versions of the F-35: the F-35A (conventional takeoff), F-35B (short takeoff and vertical landing), and F-35C (carrier operations). The U.S. plans for the F-35 to become a central part of its Air Force and Navy fleets, with NATO partners such as the UK, Italy, Australia, Canada, and Turkey also set to acquire it. This milestone event is part of a two-week sea test concluding November 17, giving military officials vital data on the aircraft’s performance and allowing for necessary adjustments before expected service entry in 2018. Commander Tony Wilson, the Navy test pilot who executed the landing, referred to it as a landmark in the program, while Vice Admiral David Buss celebrated the historic integration of next-generation technology into carrier aviation. A second F-35C is expected shortly for further flight operations. Both jets will conduct trials involving catapult launches and arrested landings, continuing assessment of the improved tailhook system. These tests inaugurate a series of three planned phases to ready the F-35C for service. Advanced stealth features make the F-35 hard to detect by radar while enabling flight at up to Mach 1.6 (1,217 mph), with an operational ceiling of 50,000 feet, measuring 51 feet in length and a 35-foot wingspan. The pilot dons a helmet with an immersive 360-degree display showing battlefield data, targeting markers, and real-time info, plus interactive screens for rapid data sharing with allied units. Earlier this year, the fleet was grounded after engine issues—a cracked rotor blade and fire—prompted further investigations. Lieutenant General Chris Bogdan, head of the program, highlighted the extensive groundwork leading up to these pivotal sea trials. Overall, this event is viewed as a positive and necessary breakthrough for the F-35 program, signaling the introduction of cutting-edge air power, even as past setbacks and budget overruns are acknowledged.

O caça utilizou um sistema de gancho de cauda redesenhado várias vezes — aparelho essencial que prende os cabos do convés para parar o avião — devido a dificuldades no desenvolvimento. An investigation has revealed that approximately 50 Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) patrol cars had their audio recording devices deliberately disabled. All LAPD patrol vehicles are outfitted with equipment that automatically records what officers say while outside their cars. However, in one South Los Angeles division, antennas for the audio system were missing from half of the estimated 80 vehicles, and another division reported 10 antennas removed.

These audio recording devices, along with in-car cameras that activate when emergency lights and sirens are engaged, are designed to protect both officers and the public by deterring malpractice and guarding against false accusations. The system works by transmitting an officer’s voice via a small device worn on their belt, which is received by in-car equipment. Removing the antenna does not necessarily prevent recording but significantly reduces the system's range—by up to one-third, according to LAPD equipment expert Sgt. Dan Gomez.

Of particular concern is that many of the cars affected patrol areas such as Watts, Jordan Downs, and Nickerson Gardens—communities where police relations can be especially strained. LAPD’s Police Commission President, Steve Soboroff, stressed the importance of the equipment, saying, 'This equipment is for the protection of the public and officers. For someone to disable it is very troubling.'

LAPD leaders were informed of the tampering in the summer of 2013 but chose not to pursue those responsible, considering it futile since multiple teams use the same vehicles. Instead, the department implemented a system to log antenna status between shifts and issued warnings. Chief Charlie Beck informed the Police Commission in September that the issue was being addressed. However, a recent investigation into a February shooting, during which audio recordings from the scene varied widely in quality, suggests the problem has not been fully resolved. Police leaders remain deeply concerned, especially given the impact on accountability in areas with challenging police-community relations.

article_content: Itzcoatl Ocampo, a 23-year-old former Marine who served in Iraq, has been accused of killing four homeless individuals in Orange County, California. Friends and family describe Ocampo as someone who was once friendly, generous, and outgoing, but say his demeanor changed significantly after his return from military service. Brian, a neighbor and longtime friend, recalled that Ocampo became more serious, withdrawn, and appeared troubled, noting signs of depression. Ocampo’s father, Refugio, expressed disbelief over his son's alleged involvement, highlighting that Ocampo was known for giving money to those in need and displaying compassion for the homeless. The family has experienced hardship—after losing their home in 2008, Ocampo’s father now lives in the cab of a semi-trailer. Refugio mentioned that after Iraq, Ocampo began expressing thoughts that didn’t make sense, such as talking about the end of the world. Police have not yet presented detailed evidence, and Ocampo has not been arraigned. Military officials have not responded to inquiries about Ocampo’s service. Both Brian and Refugio agree that the person Ocampo became after Iraq was markedly different from the young man they both knew—making the allegations difficult for them to comprehend.

article_content: The Chesapeake Bay's summer 'dead zone' in 2023 was the smallest recorded since monitoring began in 1985, according to researchers in Maryland and Virginia. Experts attribute this improvement to lower-than-average rainfall, which resulted in fewer pollutants—like nitrogen and phosphorus from farms, lawns, and urban runoff—entering the bay. These pollutants typically trigger algae blooms which, when decomposing, deplete oxygen and create dead zones. Although the dry weather caused moderate drought in much of Maryland, it provided a temporary reduction in pollution, offering relief to wildlife that struggles in low-oxygen waters. Scientists are hopeful that the pattern of smaller dead zones over the last four years signals that nutrient reduction strategies are having a positive impact. Despite experiencing warmer temperatures in 2023—which usually worsen oxygen depletion because warm water holds less oxygen—the bay recorded historically low levels of hypoxic (low-oxygen) water. Wind conditions were average, but significant storms, which typically help mix oxygen deeper into the bay, did not play a major role. Mark Trice, program chief of water quality informatics at the Maryland Department of Natural Resources, remarked that despite pressures from warmer temperatures and an increasing population, positive environmental results are still being achieved. States bordering the Chesapeake Bay pledged to reduce nutrient pollution by 2025, but most—including Maryland—are not on track to hit their targets. While early advances were made by updating sewage treatment plants, experts warn that much greater progress is needed in controlling pollution from agriculture, livestock, and stormwater runoff from impervious urban surfaces. From 2009 to 2022, the bay states achieved 51% of nitrogen reduction and 60% of phosphorus reduction goals, according to estimates by the Chesapeake Bay Program. However, a recent report from the program’s Scientific and Technical Advisory Committee found that, so far, improvements in dissolved oxygen levels—especially in the bay’s deepest areas—are slower than anticipated. The report advised focusing additional efforts on shallower tributaries for more attainable improvements. In response to these findings, Maryland Governor Wes Moore stated that his administration will adjust bay cleanup strategies according to scientific recommendations. The past few years have marked improvement following 2019, when heavy rainfall led to the largest dead zone in decades, harming oysters, crabs, and underwater grass. To monitor the dead zone, researchers collect water samples twice monthly from May to October. These data are analyzed using computer models to estimate overall conditions across the bay. Maryland estimated that in 2023, the volume of low-oxygen water in the bay's main stem was 0.52 cubic miles, while Virginia researchers estimated 0.58 cubic miles—both significantly below the historical average of 0.97 cubic miles. The low-oxygen area was centralized near the Bay Bridge and the bay's main stem through the summer and did not spread as widely as in some past years. From May through August, hypoxic water coverage was below average, and early August levels set a new record for that time of year. September saw a brief increase, but by October, researchers found no hypoxic water. Preceding this summer's data, Baltimore experienced an unusually snowless winter and a dry spring. From January to June, only 14.33 inches of precipitation were recorded at BWI Thurgood Marshall Airport, versus the typical 21.21 inches. This reduced the inflow of freshwater to the bay: from October 2022 to September 2023, inflows averaged 65,649 cubic feet per second, compared to the long-term average of 79,000 cubic feet per second. However, recent years’ water flows have generally been considered normal, and dead zone conditions continue to improve compared to historical averages. Trice concluded, 'While there are both positive and negative stories about the bay, this hopeful report shows progress, and it's important to keep up the momentum with sustained management efforts.'

Esses poluentes normalmente provocam florações de algas que, ao se decompor, consomem oxigênio e criam zonas mortas. Apesar do clima seco ter causado seca moderada em grande parte de Maryland, houve uma redução temporária da poluição, trazendo alívio à vida silvestre que sofre em águas com pouco oxigênio. Cientistas estão otimistas de que a sequência de zonas mortas menores nos últimos quatro anos indica que as estratégias de redução de nutrientes estão tendo efeito positivo. Apesar das temperaturas mais quentes em 2023—que normalmente pioram a falta de oxigênio, já que águas quentes retêm menos oxigênio—a baía registrou níveis historicamente baixos de água hipóxica (com pouco oxigênio). Os ventos foram de intensidade média, sem grandes tempestades, que normalmente ajudam a misturar oxigênio nas camadas mais profundas da baía. Mark Trice, chefe do programa de informática de qualidade da água no Departamento de Recursos Naturais de Maryland, comentou que, apesar das pressões de temperaturas mais altas e do crescimento populacional, resultados ambientais positivos ainda estão sendo alcançados. Os estados ao redor da Baía de Chesapeake se comprometeram a reduzir a poluição por nutrientes até 2025, mas a maioria—including Maryland—ainda não está no caminho certo para atingir as metas. Embora avanços iniciais tenham acontecido com a modernização de estações de tratamento de esgoto, especialistas alertam que é necessário avançar muito mais no controle da poluição da agropecuária e do escoamento das águas urbanas. Entre 2009 e 2022, os estados da baía alcançaram 51% da meta de redução de nitrogênio e 60% da meta de redução de fósforo, segundo estimativas do Programa da Baía de Chesapeake. Contudo, um relatório recente do Comitê Consultivo Científico e Técnico do programa indicou que, até agora, as melhorias nos níveis de oxigênio dissolvido—principalmente nas áreas mais profundas da baía—estão ocorrendo mais lentamente do que o esperado. O relatório recomendou esforços adicionais nos tributários mais rasos, onde melhorar as condições pode ser mais viável. Em resposta a essas descobertas, o governador de Maryland, Wes Moore, afirmou que sua administração irá ajustar as estratégias de recuperação da baía conforme as recomendações científicas. Os últimos anos têm mostrado melhorias após 2019, quando chuvas intensas causaram a maior zona morta em décadas, prejudicando ostras, caranguejos e vegetação subaquática. Para monitorar a zona morta, pesquisadores coletam amostras de água duas vezes por mês de maio a outubro. Esses dados são analisados com modelos computacionais para estimar as condições gerais da baía. Maryland estimou que, em 2023, o volume de água com pouco oxigênio na parte principal da baía foi de 0,52 milhas cúbicas, enquanto pesquisadores da Virgínia estimaram 0,58 milhas cúbicas—bem abaixo da média histórica de 0,97 milhas cúbicas. A área de baixo oxigênio ficou concentrada perto da Bay Bridge e do canal principal da baía durante o verão e não se espalhou tanto quanto em anos anteriores. De maio a agosto, a cobertura de água hipóxica ficou abaixo da média, e os níveis no início de agosto foram os melhores já registrados para essa época do ano. Setembro teve um aumento temporário, mas em outubro os pesquisadores não encontraram áreas hipóxicas. Antes dos dados deste verão, Baltimore teve um inverno praticamente sem neve e uma primavera seca. De janeiro a junho, foram registrados apenas 36,4 cm de chuva no Aeroporto BWI Thurgood Marshall, contra os 53,9 cm típicos. Isso reduziu o fluxo de água doce para a baía: de outubro de 2022 a setembro de 2023, a média foi de 1.859 metros cúbicos por segundo, contra a média de longo prazo de 2.237 metros cúbicos por segundo. No entanto, os fluxos de água dos últimos anos têm sido considerados normais, e as condições da zona morta continuam melhorando em relação à média histórica. Trice concluiu: 'Mesmo com notícias positivas e negativas sobre a baía, este relatório mostra progresso e destaca a importância de manter o compromisso com as ações de gestão.'

article_content: During a brief visit to Paris, New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio honored the victims of recent terrorist attacks. He placed a wreath at the Hyper Cacher supermarket, the site where four hostages were murdered in an anti-Semitic attack. The incident, which occurred on January 9, was carried out by Amedy Coulibaly, who was subsequently killed by police. The victims remembered were Yohan Cohen, Yoav Hattab, Francois-Michel Saada, and Phillipe Braham. Mayor de Blasio's trip included stops at other key locations impacted by the violence, such as the Charlie Hebdo offices—where he also laid a wreath—and the site where police officer Ahmed Merbat was killed. De Blasio met with Paris Mayor Anne Hidalgo to reaffirm New York’s support for France in the struggle against terrorism and anti-Semitism. A statement issued during the visit highlighted unity, quoting de Blasio: 'The mayor stands with our friends in Paris and throughout France. We will oppose terrorism and anti-Semitism together, standing up for free expression.' His visit followed U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry’s delayed trip to France, which took place after criticism that the U.S. had not initially shown sufficient support after the attacks. Meanwhile, de Blasio continues to deal with significant challenges at home, including rising tensions with the NYPD, especially in the wake of the murders of officers Rafael Ramos and Wenjian Liu amid debates over law enforcement practices.

article_content: Washington (CNN) – The Navy’s chief of operations stated Wednesday that recent budget cuts and sequestration did not influence the Navy’s decision to use an external company to screen contractors for base access. This clarification came in response to a federal audit that criticized the Rapidgate program, operated by Eid Passport, for major security weaknesses. The audit, released Tuesday, identified security problems so significant that auditors recommended immediately shutting down the Navy Commercial Access Control System (NCACS). The report found that dozens of convicted felons received unescorted access to Navy installations for periods ranging from weeks to years because the company provided temporary credentials before background checks were complete. The Pentagon inspector general’s report also noted that the NCACS, designed as a cost-saving measure, likely ended up increasing government expenditures. The release of the audit followed by one day a deadly shooting at the Washington Navy Yard. Although Aaron Alexis, the shooter, did not use NCACS credentials, the issue raised wider concerns about military base security. Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel ordered a review of security at all U.S. military installations in response. The Navy stressed that there was no link between the NCACS and Aaron Alexis, the 34-year-old IT contractor responsible for the shooting. Alexis used a different type of access credential, not provided through NCACS. Despite this, the audit uncovered security vulnerabilities at 10 sampled Navy installations out of more than 60 bases in the continental U.S. At a committee hearing, Adm. Jonathan Greenert said the Navy would cooperate with the inspector general to review recommendations but did not commit to implementing all of them. He emphasized that using an outside company was a cost-control measure unrelated to budget cuts, stating, 'We don’t cut budgetary corners for security.' Several members of Congress expressed concern. Sen. Claire McCaskill of Missouri called for the program’s immediate discontinuation, highlighting wasted funds and security dangers. Rep. Mike Turner of Ohio also voiced alarms, noting the ongoing risks to people at Navy facilities while the NCACS system operates. In its response, the Navy agreed to review and analyze some recommendations but declined the suggestion to stop the program, affirming it meets all federal background check standards. The Navy argued that discontinuing NCACS would result in unnecessary delays at base entry points. Audit data indicated that by March, over 30,000 companies and about 300,000 contractors were enrolled in NCACS. Many received interim passes before full background checks were done, and some got permanent access without being fully vetted. Most of the bases reviewed lacked the resources to properly screen contractors applying for day passes outside the NCACS system.
translated_content: Washington (CNN) – O chefe de operações da Marinha afirmou na quarta-feira que os recentes cortes orçamentários e a contenção de gastos não influenciaram a decisão da Marinha de utilizar uma empresa externa para checar o acesso de contratados às bases. Essa explicação foi dada em resposta a uma auditoria federal que criticou o programa Rapidgate, operado pela Eid Passport, por graves falhas de segurança. A auditoria, divulgada na terça-feira, apontou problemas de segurança tão sérios que recomendou o encerramento imediato do Navy Commercial Access Control System (NCACS). O relatório constatou que dezenas de pessoas condenadas receberam acesso não supervisionado a instalações da Marinha por períodos que iam de semanas a anos porque a empresa forneceu credenciais temporárias antes de concluir as verificações de antecedentes. O relatório do inspetor geral do Pentágono também apontou que o NCACS, criado como uma medida para economizar recursos, provavelmente causou aumento dos gastos governamentais. A divulgação da auditoria ocorreu um dia após um tiroteio fatal no Washington Navy Yard. Embora Aaron Alexis, o atirador, não tenha usado credenciais do NCACS, o caso trouxe à tona preocupações mais amplas sobre a segurança em bases militares. Em resposta, o secretário de Defesa Chuck Hagel ordenou uma revisão das medidas de segurança em todas as instalações militares dos EUA. A Marinha enfatizou que não houve ligação entre o NCACS e Aaron Alexis, o contratado de TI de 34 anos responsável pelo ataque. Alexis tinha outro tipo de credencial de acesso, não fornecida pelo NCACS. Apesar disso, a auditoria apontou vulnerabilidades de segurança em 10 instalações analisadas, de um total de mais de 60 bases no território continental americano. Em uma audiência, o almirante Jonathan Greenert afirmou que a Marinha iria cooperar com o inspetor geral para revisar as recomendações, mas não se comprometeu a adotar todas elas. Ele reforçou que a contratação da empresa externa foi uma medida para controle de custos, não relacionada a cortes no orçamento, afirmando: 'Não economizamos com segurança.' Diversos membros do Congresso manifestaram preocupação. A senadora Claire McCaskill, do Missouri, pediu a descontinuação imediata do programa, destacando gastos desnecessários e riscos para a segurança. O deputado Mike Turner, de Ohio, também manifestou preocupação, observando riscos contínuos às pessoas nas instalações da Marinha enquanto o sistema NCACS estiver em operação. Em sua resposta, a Marinha concordou em revisar e analisar algumas das recomendações, mas rejeitou a interrupção do programa, alegando que ele atende a todos os padrões federais para checagem de antecedentes. Segundo a Marinha, encerrar o NCACS causaria atrasos desnecessários na entrada das bases. Os dados da auditoria mostraram que, em março, mais de 30 mil empresas e cerca de 300 mil contratados estavam cadastrados no NCACS. Muitos receberam passes temporários antes do término das verificações completas e alguns obtiveram acesso permanente sem a devida checagem. A maioria das bases revisadas não dispunha de recursos suficientes para verificar os antecedentes de contratados que solicitavam passes diários fora do sistema NCACS.
